# LANXTOR E1

> E1 by Lanxtor LLC is plant engineering software for production and power plants: FEED, process, P&IDs, instrumentation, electrical, automation and maintenance on one data model (a single source of truth), cloud native and AI native, with Alex, the AI co-engineer.

Lanxtor LLC, 7545 Irvine Center Drive, Suite 200, Irvine, California 92618, USA. Email info@lanxtor.com, sales sales@lanxtor.com and support support@lanxtor.com. LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/lanxtor/

## Solutions

One page per area of E1, with what it does, how and questions engineers ask:

- [FEED and process engineering on one plant model](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-feed-process-engineering.html): FEED and process engineering in E1: PFDs with real equipment and streams, heat and material balance tables, P&IDs made from the PFD and a live line list.
- [P&IDs and instrumentation, connected to the process](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-pid-instrumentation.html): P&ID software for instrumentation engineers: instruments as tagged objects, an instrument index from the drawing, loop diagrams, datasheets and hookups.
- [Electrical design on the same plant model](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-electrical-design.html): Electrical design in E1: single line diagrams with real cables, circuit diagrams, motor starters, cable schedule, cable routes, cabinet heat and a load list.
- [Automation and control, from the same plant model](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-automation-control.html): Automation engineering in E1: signals from wiring typicals, I/O allocation, the I/O list for the DCS or PLC vendor, cause and effect, SIL and alarms.
- [One plant data model, a single source of truth](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-single-data-model.html): E1 keeps process, instrumentation, electrical and automation data in one plant data model: one object per pump, shown on every drawing, list and datasheet.
- [Predictive engineering with Alex, the AI co-engineer](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-ai-predictive-engineering.html): Alex, E1's AI co-engineer, reviews your P&ID as you draw, suggests the next symbols and learns your company's conventions. Local, and always under your control.
- [Simulate, validate and explore your design](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-simulate-validate.html): E1 simulates process lines and electrical networks on the drawing, checks every object as you work and lets you compare design options before you issue them.
- [Work across disciplines on one project](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-multidiscipline-collaboration.html): In E1, process, I&C, electrical and automation engineers work on one project at the same time, see each other's changes live and keep ownership of their scope.
- [Built for refinery-size projects](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-large-projects.html): E1 is load-tested on a refinery-size project: 498,000 objects, 1,300 dense P&IDs and 50 engineers at once on one server, with changes shared in about a second.
- [Across companies on one project](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-cross-company-projects.html): Share a live E1 project between owner, EPC contractor and specialists: each company manages its own people and licenses, within the roles and data you allow.
- [Branches for scenarios and modifications](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-branches-modifications.html): Branches in E1: change part of a design while main stays as it is, resolve conflicts, review it, push it back as one change, or split commissioning packages.
- [Revisions, datasheets and reports](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-revisions-datasheets-reports.html): E1 makes lists, reports, instrument datasheets and drawings from the model, with revision control, sign-off, change clouds and issued PDFs that never change.
- [Brownfield engineering and plant modifications, on the plant you already have](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-maintenance-brownfield.html): Brownfield engineering in E1: import legacy P&IDs from DXF, PDF, DEXPI and Excel, record as-built wiring, and run plant modifications in branches.
- [Cloud plant engineering software, with nothing to install on servers](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-cloud-workspace.html): E1 Cloud is plant engineering software as a service: sign in, invite your team and work on shared projects, hosted by LANXTOR on Microsoft Azure in the EU.
- [Your data, your deployment: E1 in your own cloud or data centre](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-enterprise-deployment.html): Run E1 in your own Microsoft Azure or on-premises on your own servers, with your own PostgreSQL database, company sign-on and an offline-checked license file.
- [Windows and macOS desktop app, browser and tablet: one project everywhere](https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-desktop-browser-tablet.html): Engineer in E1's desktop app for Windows and macOS or in the browser, and review on a laptop or tablet: the same project, the same account, nothing to sync.

# Solutions in full

## FEED and process engineering on one plant model

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-feed-process-engineering.html

In E1, the process flow diagram, the heat and material balance, the P&IDs and the line list are views of one plant model. Equipment and streams are objects with tags and values, not lines on a sheet. Instrumentation, piping, electrical and automation engineers work on the same objects, so the FEED deliverables they inherit are never retyped.

### Process flow diagrams made of real objects

In E1, a process flow diagram is a 2D space whose diagram type is Process flow diagram. Every symbol on it is an object in the project.

You place equipment from the Add asset window, and each symbol becomes a new object with the next free tag from the project's tag rules, such as P-001 and P-002 for pumps. Streams are drawn as process lines with the Connector tool, and every line is an object that connects what it touches. Unit operations, systems, processes and areas are made from the drawing toolbar while you draw.

Because the drawing and the data are the same thing, the PFD answers questions directly. Highlight flow traces where a stream goes, from an open end through valves to the next equipment, and on through pumps and compressors and across off-page connectors to other 2D spaces. Animate flow sets the sheet in motion: the flow moves through the pipes the way it goes, tanks fill and empty, and Alex works out velocities from the values in the model without changing anything.

E1 draws its own symbols for process equipment, valves and fittings in the conventions process engineers know. You browse and search them in Configuration → Shapes.

### Deep view: follow a stream through the model

Deep view shows an object and every object associated with it, as a data model of cards and links, like an object diagram rather than a drawing. You open it layer by layer with +1, or all at once with Expand all, until nothing more is linked.

From the HP separator 20-VA-2001 you follow its pipe runs to the valves on them, its pipeline and piping segments, the PFD, P&ID and datasheet that show it, and the HAZOP tasks raised on it, to see everything it touches before you change it.

Click a card to see its values and links, with Open, Show in tree and Deep view of this. Highlight route draws the way from one card to another in bold while everything else fades; Find in view outlines the cards whose tag, name, class or value holds your text; a chip for each kind of link shows or hides those links.

- Opened from the object window's Deep view tab, or from a symbol on a 2D space: right-click → Open ▸ Deep view.

### Heat and material balance from the line list

In E1, the heat and material balance tables on a PFD are made from the line list. Nothing in a table is typed.

Stream values come into the line list in three ways: typed, imported from your simulator, or written by Alex from a solved balance. Import heat and material balance in Alex reads the stream table of HYSYS, Aspen Plus, DWSIM or a similar simulator as .xlsx, .xls, .csv or .txt. Alex matches streams to lines by name or by the middle of the line number, you check each match, and only then are the values written. Alex then asks only for what is still missing.

On the PFD, Place mass balance draws the bird cage: one column per stream with line number, From, To, phase, temperature, pressure, flows, density, molar mass and composition. Place heat balance lists every heater, cooler, exchanger, pump and compressor with its service, duty and power, and the totals. Format presets set the layout your customer expects, and a changed temperature in the line list shows in the table at once.

- A value that is missing, or cannot be shown in the chosen unit, shows as – rather than a guess.

### Make the P&ID from the PFD

In E1, Make P&ID from this PFD… draws a new P&ID with the PFD's own equipment: the same objects with the same tags, not copies.

Each stream becomes a pipe between the same equipment, carrying the same stream. You choose which objects to draw; one already on a P&ID of that PFD, or with no P&ID shape, is greyed with the reason. Equipment you leave for a second P&ID ends at an off-page connector that continues there. Nothing is drawn twice.

When objects or streams are added to the PFD later, Update from PFD offers only the new ones. The new P&ID opens with Alex's Suggested additions: what each object usually has on a P&ID. A centrifugal pump gets suction and discharge isolation, a discharge check valve, a suction strainer and a discharge pressure gauge; a vessel gets a relief valve, a drain, a vent, level and pressure instruments. Additions your company's conventions require come first, and Apply all is one change with one Undo.

### Pipelines, pipe classes and a live line list

In E1, a pipeline is a line of the line list: the pipe runs, valves and fittings from one equipment nozzle to another, with its line number, From and To.

You define a pipeline on the drawing from one item of equipment to the next, and E1 follows the drawn pipe through valves and fittings to make it, split into segments at reducers. A pipeline names its pipe class. Pipe classes hold your piping specifications: rating, material, pressure–temperature envelope, sizes with their schedule, and the valves and fittings allowed. They are kept in the company or project library, published as versions, and can be imported from a spreadsheet.

Check piping… finds a pump turned the wrong way, flow that meets head-on, branches with only inflow, and pipelines that are no longer whole. It offers fixes and never applies one on its own. With pipe classes loaded, Alex checks each line's pressure and temperature against its class and flags sour service in a class not rated for it.

E1 ships no fixed line list. The pipe schedule is a query you build and save on the project's pipelines: line number, From and To, size, fluid, pipe class, design conditions and the P&IDs each line is drawn on. It stays live with the drawing and exports to Excel or CSV, or becomes a list document with revisions.

### FEED deliverables that downstream disciplines inherit

In E1, datasheets, lists and drawings are generated from the same objects, so the FEED package and the detailed design never drift apart.

Specification datasheets for pumps and exchangers come as ready-made templates, E1's own layouts inspired by API and ASME datasheets. Operating cases sit side by side on the datasheet: maximum, rated, normal, minimum, design or start-up, each inheriting the object's values until you give it its own. After a datasheet is issued, every value changed since shows the next revision beside it.

Documents → Deliverables binds the chosen drawings with the reports and datasheets of the deliverable profile into one PDF, with a cover, an index and page numbers, and issues it. Process data also leaves E1 as data: any query exports to Excel, CSV or JSON, a 2D space exports as DEXPI 2.0 for a 3D design tool or another P&ID tool, and existing P&IDs come in from DEXPI, DXF or a vector PDF.

### Questions

**Does E1 replace a process simulator?** No. E1 keeps the results of your simulator in the plant model. Import heat and material balance reads a stream table from HYSYS, Aspen Plus, DWSIM or a similar tool into the line list, and the balance tables on the PFD are made from it.

**Is the P&ID a copy of the PFD?** No. Make P&ID from this PFD… draws the PFD's own equipment objects with their P&ID shapes, with the same tags. A change to a pump's data is the same change on both drawings.

**What happens when the PFD changes after the P&ID is made?** Update from PFD appears on the P&ID with only the new objects and streams ticked. What is already drawn is not drawn twice.

**Can I format the mass balance the way my customer wants?** Yes. Format mass balance has presets, one row or one column per stream, the composition left of or below the properties, and a unit per property. The table always shows the line list's current values.

**Does E1 come with a fixed line list?** No. You build the pipe schedule as a saved query with the rows and columns you need, and it is offered in every Query menu of the project. It exports to Excel or CSV, or becomes a revised list document.

**Can I bring existing P&IDs into E1?** Yes: DEXPI 2.0 files, DXF from CAD and vector PDFs exported from CAD become drawings with real objects. You check the result before anything is stored. A scanned image cannot be read.

## P&IDs and instrumentation, connected to the process

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-pid-instrumentation.html

In E1, every instrument on a P&ID is an object in the plant model with its tag, its values and its relationships. The instrument index, the loop diagrams, the instrument datasheets and the hookups are made from those objects. Change an instrument once and the drawing, the lists and the documents agree.

### P&ID software where every symbol is an object

In E1, placing an instrument, valve or item of equipment on a P&ID creates an object in the project with the next free tag from the project's tag rules.

E1 draws its own symbols for instruments, control valves and logic as well as for equipment, valves and fittings. You find them in the Add asset window by name, type, class or diagram type, and two clicks set a symbol's inlet and outlet as you place it. The Connector tool draws pipes, signal lines and cables point by point, and each line connects what it touches. Symbols show their tags and pipe runs their line numbers.

Tags follow the project's rules, with reference designations. When an input of a rule changes, the tag is marked out of date instead of changing behind your back, and Retag… shows every old and new tag before it applies them. While Alex is on, placing a pump brings an offer of what usually comes next, drawn as ghost symbols you apply or reject.

- Engineering patterns draw a control valve station or an instrument tap at once, placed, routed and checked (with an AI model set up for Alex).
- Existing P&IDs come in from DEXPI 2.0, DXF or a vector PDF as real objects, checked by you before anything is stored.

### Deep view: follow an instrument from the field to the I/O channel

Deep view shows an object and every object associated with it, as a data model of cards and links, like an object diagram rather than a drawing. You open it layer by layer with +1, or all at once with Expand all, until nothing more is linked.

From LIT 2001 you follow its loop, its cable 76-W-LIT2001, the cores landed on its terminals and the terminal strip in junction box JB-20-01, as well as its alarms and its hookup, and Highlight route shows the way in bold.

Click a card to see its values and links, with Open, Show in tree and Deep view of this. Highlight route draws the way from one card to another in bold while everything else fades; Find in view outlines the cards whose tag, name, class or value holds your text; a chip for each kind of link shows or hides those links.

- Opened from the object window's Deep view tab, or from a symbol on a 2D space: right-click → Open ▸ Deep view.

### An instrument index that is never out of date

In E1, the instrument index is read from the model, so it lists exactly the instruments that are on the drawings and in the project.

Alex's Export instrument index (Excel) reads the instruments, signals and motors on a 2D space and writes the instrument index, the I/O list, the cause and effect and the motor list into one workbook, one sheet per list. If your company uploaded its list column templates in Alex knowledge, the columns follow them.

For the project as a whole, an instrument list is a saved query with the columns you choose. It exports to Excel, CSV or JSON with an E1 id column. Update from Excel… reads an edited file back: Check lists every change row by row, and Apply makes them in one undoable step. An instrument list from another tool comes in with Import Excel…: matching rows are updated and the others become new objects. Up to 100 instruments of one class are made in one go from the New object window.

### Loop diagrams generated from the model

In E1, a loop diagram is drawn from the model whenever you look at it: the instruments that implement a control function and the devices it controls, in signal order, with their wiring.

Right-click a function such as TIC-101 and choose Preview loop diagram, or pick several to preview them on one temporary sheet. Nothing is stored while you preview. Export a PDF to send it, or create a version or a revision: only then is each loop stored in Documents, where you can move symbols by hand and Regenerate keeps your moves.

The loop diagram follows each circuit from the device through the junction boxes, cables, marshalling and barriers to the I/O channel, with the barrier's power feed and the screens to their earth bar. Every terminal is drawn in a column by zone: junction box, marshalling field side, interposing, marshalling system side, I/O, and supply and earth. Wiring that is still under way is shown as far as it goes, so loop diagrams are useful from the first day of detailed design.

### Instrument datasheets on the same objects

In E1, an instrument datasheet is a view of the instrument's own values: type into the datasheet and the object changes.

Ready-made specification datasheets for instruments and valves are E1's own templates inspired by ISA datasheets, such as the electromagnetic flowmeter specification. Lines are numbered, tables of parts continue on continuation pages, units are added and checked, and the PDF looks the same as the screen. The datasheet designer copies a template into your own layout, which can later take over changes from it.

One datasheet document can cover several tags of one class. Shared values show once, values that differ show See list, and one change sets all of them. After a datasheet document is issued, every value changed since shows the next revision beside it, so the next issue is easy to review.

### Hookups, hookup drawings and the hookup schedule

In E1, a hookup shows how an instrument is fixed and connected, and every instrument installed the same way uses the same hookup.

Turn hookups on for a project and they get a folder of their own, Assets ▸ Hookups, with their type, mounting, drawing and bill of material. On every instrument you choose the hookup it uses, and every hookup shows the instruments that use it.

A hookup drawing is made from the model: an arrangement sketch with a balloon per part, the bill of material, the instruments that use it and notes, on one A3 page with the title block. The hookup schedule lists every hookup with its instruments and the material they need in total, exported to PDF and Excel and revised and issued like any other document.

### Questions

**Is the instrument index a separate database from the P&ID?** No. The instrument on the P&ID and the row in the instrument index are the same object. The index is read from the model each time you export it.

**Do loop diagrams need finished wiring?** No. A loop diagram shows the wiring that is there. As cores are landed on junction boxes, marshalling and I/O channels, the next preview shows them.

**Are the datasheet templates copies of ISA forms?** No. Only the idea comes from ISA, API and ASME specification datasheets. The layout, sections, wording and line numbers are E1's own, with no form names, numbers or logos of theirs.

**Can I use my company's own datasheet layout?** Yes. Copy a template, or build a layout from components in the datasheet designer, preview it with several objects and publish it for a class.

**Can I import an existing instrument list?** Yes. Import Excel… brings an Excel or CSV tag list into a section: matching rows are updated and the others become new objects, after a preview.

**How are tags given to new instruments?** From the project's tag rules, built from segments, lookup tables and options. A manual tag can be set with Tag…, and Retag… brings out-of-date tags back in line after a preview.

## Electrical design on the same plant model

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-electrical-design.html

In E1, the electrical engineer works on the same objects as process and instrumentation: the motor of a pump, the cabinet in an equipment room, the cable between them. Single line diagrams, circuit diagrams, the cable schedule and the electrical documents are made from that model, so plant power is not a separate island of tools.

### Single line diagrams where every line is a real cable

In E1, a single line diagram is a 2D space whose diagram type is Single line diagram. Field devices, junction boxes and cabinets are objects of the model, and every line drawn between them with Cable is a real cable.

Each cable you draw has its tag, the project's default cable type for its two ends and its cores. It is the same cable the cable schedule and the wiring show. Default cable types are set once in the project's wiring settings: field cable, multicore, cabinet to cabinet and feeder.

Propose cables designs the cable network for new devices in one step. For every field device on the sheet that has signals and no field cable, E1 proposes a field cable to the nearest junction box of its area and segregation class with room on a strip. Free pairs of existing multicores are used first; a new multicore or junction box is proposed only where none fits. Nothing changes until you choose Apply.

Animate current sets a single line diagram in motion: the current runs from the transformers or generators through the switchboard to the motors, coloured by voltage level. Open a breaker and its cable turns dead and the motor reads No supply. Nothing in the model changes.

### Deep view: follow a motor to its cable, starter and breaker

Deep view shows an object and every object associated with it, as a data model of cards and links, like an object diagram rather than a drawing. You open it layer by layer with +1, or all at once with Expand all, until nothing more is linked.

From motor 43-EM-4301A you follow its power cable 80-P-021 to circuit breaker 80-EQ-4301A, the cable from there to the motor control centre 80-EN-8001, and the pump it drives.

Click a card to see its values and links, with Open, Show in tree and Deep view of this. Highlight route draws the way from one card to another in bold while everything else fades; Find in view outlines the cards whose tag, name, class or value holds your text; a chip for each kind of link shows or hides those links.

- Opened from the object window's Deep view tab, or from a symbol on a 2D space: right-click → Open ▸ Deep view.

### Circuit diagrams and motor starter circuits

In E1, each symbol on a circuit diagram is one function of a device: a contactor's coil, its contacts and main poles, a pushbutton's contact, a pilot light's lamp.

The device is one object owned by its cabinet, and its catalog item gives its functions with their terminal markings (A1 A2, 13 14, 21 22). Every drawn function has an address by page and column, such as /1.4. Under a contactor's coil E1 shows the contact image: each contact with its points and where it is drawn. E1 works these out from the drawings, so they are never out of date.

Right-click a motor and choose Make starter circuit…: E1 draws the starter on a new page of its cabinet's circuit document, with the motor protection breaker, contactor and overload relay in the three phases, the control circuit with its fuse, Stop, Start and pilot lights, the motor's terminals and its power cable. The breaker, contactor and overload relay are the catalog's smallest that take the motor's current. Pick several motors to make all their starters at once.

Terminals, cables and wire numbers are drawn on the same pages. E1 finds two potentials joined by a wire (a short circuit), more wires across a cable than it has cores, and contact points with no wire.

### Cable schedule, cable routes and lengths

In E1, a cable made from a cable type in the catalog gets its cores at once, and each core is landed on a terminal chosen from a tree, never typed.

The cable schedule is the Cables tab of the Wiring page: one row per cable with its type, its two ends, the cores used and spare, its length and its status. It exports to Excel or PDF with the wire list, termination list, junction box schedule and I/O list, all made from the model when you ask for them.

Route segments are cable trays, ladders, conduits, ducts and trenches with their capacity and fill limit. A cable is routed through segments in order; each segment's fill adds up its cables' cross-sections and the cable's routed length adds up the segments. A cable has a length by hand and a length from 3D, and E1 reports when they differ by more than the project's tolerance.

- Wire numbers from the project's pattern, with a preview of every change.
- Construction status on every core and terminal: Designed, Issued for construction, Installed, Terminated, Loop-checked, As-built or To be removed.
- After issue, a change becomes a wire move list of what to lift and what to land, terminal by terminal.

### Cabinets, MCCs, potentials and heat balance

In E1, a cabinet is two objects: its location in Areas and the enclosure in Assets, which holds rails, terminal strips, cards, interposing devices, power supplies, earth bars and cable entries. An MCC and a distribution board are enclosures too.

The Potentials tab lists every net such as +24V across enclosures, with its terminals, fuses and the supply's load against its rated current. The net view shows each fused terminal with its rating and the load it feeds; a missing value shows as ?, never as zero.

A cabinet's Fill and heat page shows each strip as a bar of used, spare and free terminals, and the heat balance from physics: the heat its devices give off at their load against what its free walls, a fan and a cooling unit take away. The result is the inside temperature, the temperature at the top, the margin to the cabinet's limit and the cooling still missing. Markers for wires, terminals and cables export for the printer's software.

### Electrical load list and electrical documents

In E1, Alex with the Electrical engineer skill writes the electrical load list, the cable schedule and the Ex equipment list of a 2D space into one Excel workbook.

Export load list and cable schedule (Excel) gives the load list with the maximum demand, the cable schedule with capacity and voltage drop, and the Ex equipment list. Alex judges cables with the ratings of IEC 60364-5-52 and a voltage drop of 3 % for lighting and 5 % for other uses. When a simulator in Alex has run an electrical load flow, short circuit, motor start or arc flash on the open 2D space, its results appear as cards with the method, inputs, assumptions and result tables.

Make documents… on a cabinet, a folder or the project makes the electrical document set in one change: terminal strip diagrams, the cable block diagram, a cable diagram per cable, the wire list, the I/O list, the device list, the parts list and the table of contents, and for the project the potential overview. They are revised and issued like any document.

### Questions

**Is a cable on the single line diagram the same as in the cable schedule?** Yes. Every line drawn with Cable on a single line diagram is the cable object itself, with its tag, type and cores. The cable schedule and the wiring show the same cable.

**How does E1 choose the starter components for a motor?** From the motor's rated output or current: the breaker, contactor and overload relay are the catalog's smallest that take that current. You choose the cabinet and the control voltage in the dialog.

**Can E1 work out cable lengths from a 3D model?** A cable keeps a length by hand and a length from 3D, written through E1's API. E1 uses the length by hand when there is one and reports when the two differ by more than the project's tolerance.

**Can I import the wiring of an existing plant or a vendor panel?** Yes. A termination list in CSV or Excel is imported through Alex with a preview first. The cores come in as fixed, so the new design is made around them.

**Does E1 calculate cabinet heat dissipation?** Yes. The Fill and heat page works out the inside and top temperature from the devices' heat loss, the free walls, a fan and a cooling unit, and says how much cooling is missing.

**Which electrical documents can E1 make?** Terminal strip diagrams, cable block and cable diagrams, wire list, I/O list, device list, parts list, table of contents and the potential overview, plus the cable schedule and the other wiring lists in Excel and PDF.

## Automation and control, from the same plant model

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-automation-control.html

In E1, signals, I/O channels, control system cabinets, the cause and effect matrix and the alarms belong to the same plant model as the P&IDs and the instruments. Automation work starts from the engineering data itself, not from a spreadsheet export, and what goes to the control-system vendor comes back into the same model.

### Signals from wiring typicals

In E1, a wiring typical describes one kind of device once, such as a 2-wire transmitter, a solenoid valve or a motor-operated valve, and gives every device that uses it its I/O signals, terminals and field cables.

A typical holds the device's signals (open command, closed limit, position and so on), its field cables and the pair each signal takes, options such as position feedback, variants, and the naming of cables and wires. Set it on many devices at once and E1 makes their signals and cables with cores landed on the device and numbered.

The Wiring page of a unit, loop, cabinet, cable or device shows every signal in one row with its whole path: field cable, junction box, multicore, marshalling and I/O channel. A dash is a place not reached yet. Trace circuit follows a circuit through cores, jumpers, barriers and isolators to the I/O channel, the power supply and the earth bar, and names every terminal by its reference designation, such as +CR1-A3-X1:5.

### Wiring allocation that keeps the rules

In E1, Propose wiring fills each signal's empty places: a junction box strip, a free multicore pair to the marshalling cabinet, and cross-wires to a free channel of its kind.

The proposal never breaks a hard rule. It keeps the control system, the project's segregation matrix and each strip's segregation class, keeps redundancy groups apart (a 2oo3 group on three junction boxes and three cards), matches the channel's type and HART, leaves fixed and reserved terminals alone, and keeps the spare percentage. Every choice says why, and every junction box it did not take says which rule it breaks. The same devices give the same proposal every time.

Nothing changes until you accept. You accept one cell, a row, a column or everything, and a hop is never accepted without the one before it, so no core is left landed at one end. When every card of the marshalling cabinet is full, the channel is proposed on a new card in the first free slot of a rack of the signal's control system.

### Racks, cards and the I/O list for the DCS or PLC vendor

In E1, a cabinet's Contents page shows each rack with its control system and every slot, the card in each slot with its channels, and the transmitter landed on each channel.

Drag a card onto a free slot to move it; its cross-wires follow. Export I/O list gives the control-system vendor every signal with its kind, segregation class, control system and HART, and the cabinet, rack, slot, card, channel and terminals its circuit reaches. Vendors often assign channels themselves. When their list comes back, Alex imports it as a preview: a channel they kept becomes fixed, and a channel they changed is a finding, where you decide whether E1 moves the cross-wires.

On a circuit diagram, an I/O card is drawn as a PLC box whose connection points are its channels' terminals, named as the I/O list names them. A contact or lamp drawn in line with one is wired to the channel at once, so the wire list and the I/O list show it.

- Fieldbus segments for Foundation Fieldbus H1 and Profibus PA, with current budget, voltages, device counts and lengths as limits a device must keep within.
- The entity check for intrinsically safe loops and the voltage budget at 20 mA, with missing values reported as missing, never as zero.

### Cause and effect, safety instrumented functions and alarms

In E1, the cause and effect matrix of a unit or loop is filled like a spreadsheet, with causes and devices chosen from lists of the project's instruments, interlocks and devices.

Each cell is set with a click or a key (C Close, O Open, S Stop, R Start), with an optional delay. Causes that vote are grouped, such as 2 of 3, and E1 writes the narrative from the matrix: when two of PT-101A, PT-101B, PT-101C read high-high above 12 bar(g), close XV-101 after 5 s. The matrix exports to the Excel workbook engineers hand over and reads back with a preview, and it is compared with any version or revision of its document.

An interlock becomes a safety instrumented function with its required SIL. Given failure rates and the proof test interval, E1 shows the PFD with the simplified low-demand equations of IEC 61508-6, the hardware fault tolerance, and whether the achieved SIL meets the requirement. Alarms are rationalized from severity and time to respond, and E1 proposes the priority after EEMUA 191 and ISA-18.2. Each plant state, such as Start-up or Shutdown, shows which alarms it suppresses.

### System control diagrams to NORSOK I-005

In E1, the NORSOK SCD content package draws system control diagrams with the function templates of NORSOK I-005, every terminal of the standard named on the block.

The package brings the function templates such as MA, CA, LB and SBV, the non-standard function, the elementary functions, references, and sequence diagrams with steps, transitions and actions. Every parameter of a function is an attribute, and every process shape that fits a P&ID fits a system control diagram too.

Check SCD… reports signals that join two outputs, an analogue output wired to a binary input, and other breaches of the standard's rules, with Show to open the place on the drawing. Function tags follow NORSOK Z-DP-002, for example 43LIC0001.

### Questions

**Does E1 program the PLC or DCS?** No. E1 prepares the engineering the control system is built from: signals, I/O allocation, the I/O list, cause and effect, safety functions and alarms. The I/O list goes to the control-system vendor and their list comes back into E1.

**What happens when the vendor changes channel assignments?** When their I/O list is imported, a kept channel becomes fixed and a changed one is a finding. You decide whether E1 moves the cross-wires to the vendor's channel.

**Is the wiring proposal repeatable?** Yes. The same devices give the same proposal every time, every choice explains why, and nothing is changed until you accept it.

**Can I keep working on the cause and effect matrix in Excel?** Yes. Export it as a workbook with its legend and narratives, edit it, and import it back: E1 lists what it will add, change and remove before anything changes, and one Undo takes the import back.

**Does the SIL calculation replace a SIL verification?** It gives the PFD, hardware fault tolerance and achieved SIL from the simplified equations of IEC 61508-6. Diagnostics, repair time and partial stroke tests are not counted, so follow your project's verification rules.

**Is NORSOK SCD switched on in every project?** No. It is off in a new project. A project administrator switches it on in Project settings → Content packages, and it switches Plant engineering and Electrical foundation on with it.

## One plant data model, a single source of truth

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-single-data-model.html

In E1, process, instrumentation, electrical and automation engineering work on one shared plant data model, from FEED to modifications. A pump is one object: the P&ID, the datasheet, the line list, the wiring and the cause and effect matrix all show that same object, so a value changed in one place is changed everywhere.

### One object, every view: what a single source of truth means in E1

In E1, every pump, valve, instrument, cable and function is one object in the project's data model, stored once on the E1 server.

A drawing in E1 does not hold its own copy of the data. A symbol on a P&ID is a placement of an object, and the same object can be drawn on several 2D spaces. The object's Diagrams tab shows a small picture of every diagram it is drawn on, with the diagram's full path; a double-click opens that diagram with the object selected and in view.

Everything else about the object is in its own window, opened from the explorer, a list or the drawing: its attributes, relationships, deep view, diagrams, datasheet, chat, history and files. An object made in a list or in the explorer is placed on a drawing later, by dragging it from the explorer or with Place on drawing…, and keeps everything it already has.

Because there is one record, there is nothing to keep in step. Attribute labels on a symbol, such as a design pressure with its unit, always show the current value: change it in a list or on the datasheet, and every 2D space and its PDF show the new value. No label text is stored.

The same holds between diagram types. Make P&ID from this PFD… draws the PFD's own equipment on a new P&ID: the same objects with the same tags, not copies, and each stream as a pipe between the same equipment. What is added to the PFD later is drawn with Update from PFD.

### A plant data model with nine sections

In E1, every project has the same nine sections in the same order: Model Space, Unit Operations, Assets, Systems, Processes, Areas, Documents, Tasks and Branches.

Each section holds one kind of thing. Model Space holds the drawings. Assets holds the equipment and instruments, and every drawn pipe run, cable, wire and signal is an object there too. Systems holds the functional breakdown, Processes the steps, fluids and operating cases, and Areas the site, plant, unit, room and cabinet. Right-clicking a section offers exactly what can be made in it.

Relationships connect objects across sections: a function under Systems “is implemented by” a pump under Assets, a transmitter “measures” the pump, a cabinet “is located in” a room. You pick the other object in a tree that shows only what fits the relationship, and every relationship shows from both sides.

Deep view shows an object and everything linked to it as cards and links, like an object diagram rather than a drawing. From a valve you follow the pipes on its ports to the pump, the transmitter that measures it, its terminals, the cable core landed on them and the junction box at the other end of the cable.

What an object can hold comes from the library: object classes, attributes, relationship types and shapes. Content packages such as Core, Electrical foundation, Plant engineering, CFIHOS and NORSOK SCD bring them ready-made, and your organization adds its own classes and attributes in the company library and publishes them to every project. Every quantity is stored with its value and its unit.

### Process, instrumentation, electrical and automation data on the same objects

In E1, each discipline adds its data to the same objects instead of keeping its own copy of the plant.

A centrifugal pump carries process data (operating and design conditions, fluid, performance), mechanical data, piping data, electrical data for its motor and hazardous area, and instrumentation data for its signals, alarms and trips. Each group is a section of the same datasheet, and each discipline fills in its own.

The pipe schedule is a query on the project's pipelines with line number, From and To, size, pipe class and design conditions, live with the drawing. A loop diagram is drawn from the model whenever you look at it, from the instruments that implement a control function and their wiring. The Wiring page shows every signal with its whole path, from the field cable to its I/O channel. The cause and effect matrix is filled on a unit in Systems, with causes and devices chosen from the model.

Because all of this reads the same objects, renaming a pump, changing its motor rating or moving a transmitter to another junction box is one change that every discipline sees. See work across disciplines for how teams share one project at the same time.

### Lists, datasheets and calculated values that follow the model

In E1, a list is a live query of the model, not an exported spreadsheet that goes out of date.

New query… opens a live table of every object below a project, section, folder, 2D space or object. You choose the columns, filter and group the rows, and edit cells like in Excel; a block pasted from Excel is previewed before anything changes. One query can also run over every project of the organization you may view.

Data still moves in and out as engineers expect. A query exports to Excel, CSV or JSON with an E1 id column, and Update from Excel… reads the file back with Check and Apply. Tag lists and data sheets are imported from Excel, P&IDs from DEXPI 2.0, DXF or PDF, and a 2D space is exported as DEXPI 2.0 for a 3D design tool or another P&ID tool.

Rules keep derived values right. A calculation rule fills an attribute from the object's own values, its owners, related objects or the project; the value follows its inputs in the same change, and Why this value? shows the rule, each input and where it came from. Nobody types a calculated value.

### Every change recorded, every change reversible

In E1, every saved change is recorded on the object it touched, with when, who, and the value before and after.

The History tab of an object lists its changes as a person reads them, and Undo this change takes one back, even an older one, as long as nobody has changed the object since. A change made by Alex, a stored assistant or an import is recorded the same way and can be undone as a group.

The E1 server is the only writer to the model and checks the permission of every change, whoever or whatever asks for it. That is what lets a whole team, and Alex, the AI co-engineer, work on one source of truth without losing track of who changed what.

### Questions

**What is a single source of truth in plant engineering?** It means every item of the plant is stored once and every drawing, list and document shows that one record. In E1, a pump is one object; the P&ID, the datasheet, the line list and the wiring all read it, so there are no copies to reconcile.

**Can one object be drawn on several drawings?** Yes. An object can be placed on several 2D spaces, and its Diagrams tab lists every diagram it is on. A PFD and the P&ID made from it draw the same equipment objects, with the same tags.

**Do I still get Excel lists?** Yes. Any query exports to Excel, CSV or JSON, and Update from Excel… reads changes back with a check before anything is applied. The list in E1 itself stays live with the model.

**Which content packages and standards does the data model use?** E1 comes with content packages such as Core, Electrical foundation, Plant engineering, CFIHOS, NORSOK SCD, Specification, Wire harness and Marine. Your organization can add its own classes and attributes in the company library.

**Can I bring in P&IDs from other tools?** Yes. E1 imports DEXPI 2.0 files, P&IDs from CAD as DXF, P&IDs exported as PDF, and tag lists and data sheets from Excel. A DEXPI import run again updates what is there instead of duplicating it.

**How large can one model be?** Our load tests run on a refinery-size project with 498,000 objects and 1,300 dense sheets. See built for refinery-size projects and the E1 Cloud specifications for the measured times.

## Predictive engineering with Alex, the AI co-engineer

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-ai-predictive-engineering.html

In E1, Alex reads the drawing as you work, the way a process, automation or electrical engineer beside you would, and suggests what usually comes next. Alex's review runs locally, with no language model and nothing sent outside E1. Every suggestion waits for you to apply or reject it.

### Alex, the AI co-engineer built into E1

In E1, Alex is one assistant in the panel on the right of the window, with three tabs: Co-engineer, Agent and E1 Guide.

In Co-engineer, Alex is built into E1. It reads the open 2D space and lists warnings, questions and suggestions. It calls no language model and sends nothing outside E1, so it works in every installation. Alex is off until you click Let Alex help, and Stop Alex switches it off again.

In Agent, Alex answers in your own words with the help of a language model and can change the project, with review and undo. E1 Guide teaches E1 where you are, with bubbles on the real buttons. The name comes from Hero of Alexandria, the first-century engineer often called the father of automation.

Alex reads the drawing when you open it and about half a second after a change of yours settles, never while you are dragging. Its marks sit on the drawing, an amber ! for a warning and a blue ? for a question, linked both ways to its cards.

### Predictive mode: the next move, suggested while you draw

In E1, while Alex is on, placing or changing something brings an offer of what usually comes next, drawn as ghost symbols on the 2D space.

Place a centrifugal pump and ghost valves appear around it. The offer is also the first card under Design suggestions, with the badge After your change and the buttons Show, Apply and Reject. Apply places the symbols as real, connected objects; Reject drops the offer and nothing is added. One undo takes an applied suggestion back.

Alex follows the design your project repeats. Where there is none yet, it uses starter rules: isolation on a pump's suction and a check valve on its discharge, isolation around control valves, and transmitters on vessels and exchangers. A pump, compressor, fan, agitator or conveyor with nothing to drive it gets the suggestion to add a motor, which is made in the model and tagged by the project's tag rules.

E1 never adds what a piece of equipment needs by itself: Alex suggests it and you decide. The same holds for a P&ID made from a PFD, which opens with Suggested additions: what each object usually has on a P&ID, for you to apply or reject.

### A design review as you work: warnings, questions and suggestions

In E1, Alex's findings are cards that say why, show where on the drawing, and offer a fix, an answer field or a way to set them aside.

The skill decides which engineer reads the drawing: Plant engineer (every discipline), Process engineer, Automation engineer, Electrical engineer or HAZOP leader. The level decides how much Alex tells you, from warnings only at Quiet to tips that explain the practice at Mentor.

Alex checks line velocity by service, pressure drop, erosional velocity and design margin, sour service and CO₂, instrument loops, tags, fail positions, interlocks against the cause and effect matrix, and anti-surge, and asks about motor starting and signal types. A question card writes your answer straight into the object. A finding that does not apply is hidden with Not applicable, or proposed to your company so Alex stops raising it once an approver accepts.

Each skill also writes its lists from the drawing into Excel: the instrument index, I/O list, cause and effect and motor list for automation; the load list, cable schedule and Ex equipment list for electrical; a prepared HAZOP worksheet with LOPA scenarios for the HAZOP leader.

### Alex learns your company's engineering conventions

In E1, Alex learns from your own standards and projects, and a rule it finds applies only after a person accepts it.

In Configuration → Alex knowledge, upload a standard as PDF, Word, Excel or text. Alex reads it locally and proposes the conventions it finds, such as a velocity limit for pump suction lines or a fail position for fuel gas control valves. Once an approver accepts one, Alex checks every drawing against it and its card quotes the clause. A language model reads the document only if you tick that option, and nothing is trained on your documents.

Team memory learns which values are usual at your company, such as the pipe class most cooling water lines get, from the projects you choose. It is off until someone with the permission switches it on, and confidential projects can be left out. With your pipe classes loaded, Alex also checks each line's pressure, temperature, class and sour service against them.

### Agent, Ask and Plan: AI for engineering design, with review and undo

In E1, Alex's Agent tab answers questions in your own words and changes the project with the same commands you run by hand.

The mode decides what Alex may do: Agent edits the project, Ask only answers and never changes anything, and Plan writes out a plan and waits for Apply. With Review changes first, Alex works on a draft that is stored only when you apply it. Protect the arrangement, on by default, lets Alex add symbols, lines and notes but not move, resize or reroute what is drawn. Undo change takes back everything one reply changed.

Some changes always wait for you: a turn that would delete more than 10 objects, and commands marked to always ask. When you ask whether a design is right, Alex's own review runs first with your accepted conventions, and the answer rests on its findings. Alex also draws engineering patterns such as a redundant pump train, answers queries such as “all pumps without a motor”, and reads attached lists, specifications and screenshots.

### Safe and secure: you and your organization stay in control

In E1, Alex works with the permissions of the person who asks, never more, and your organization sets Alex's AI help to on, answer only, or off.

Co-engineer and E1 Guide send nothing. In the Agent tab, your messages and the project context go to the model named under the tabs. In the E1 Cloud the default is GPT-4.1 on Azure OpenAI in Sweden Central, in the EU; see E1 Cloud specifications. In your own installation, the operators choose OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry or a local model server.

Restricted values are removed before anything is sent to a model, and every call to the AI is logged with its model and size, without the text of your messages. Names, notes and attached files are treated as data, never as instructions. Without a model, Alex keeps reviewing in Co-engineer and you do the rest by hand. See Security.

### Questions

**What is predictive engineering in E1?** While Alex is on, E1 offers what usually comes next after a change, such as the valves around a new pump, as ghost symbols on the drawing. You apply or reject each offer; nothing is added without you.

**Is Alex a local AI?** Alex's review in Co-engineer and the E1 Guide run inside E1, with no language model, and send nothing outside. Only the Agent tab uses a language model, and it says which one your messages go to.

**Does Alex change my drawing on its own?** No. Suggestions wait for Apply. In the Agent tab, Ask never changes anything, Plan waits for Apply, and Agent can work on a draft you review. Large deletions are always held, and one click undoes a reply.

**Which language model does Alex use?** In the E1 Cloud, GPT-4.1 on Azure OpenAI in Sweden Central is the default. An Editor may choose Claude Opus 5.5 for their own conversations; those requests may be processed outside the EU. Your own installation can use a local model server.

**Is our data used to train a model?** No. Standards you give Alex knowledge are not used for training; their matching clauses are sent with a question only in the Agent tab. Team memory is off until you switch it on, and you choose the projects it learns from.

**Can our organization switch Alex off?** Yes. The organization sets Alex's AI help to on, answer only or off. Without it, E1 works fully by hand, and Alex's local review in Co-engineer still runs.

**Does Alex replace the engineer?** No. Alex points at what an experienced colleague would notice and drafts routine work. The engineer decides what is applied, and every change Alex makes is recorded and can be undone.

## Simulate, validate and explore your design

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-simulate-validate.html

In E1, the design is checked while you work on it. Alex simulates process lines and electrical networks from the values in the model, Animate flow shows what the plant does when a pump stops or a valve closes, and every object carries its own findings. Issues are found on the drawing, early, instead of in a review months later.

### Process and electrical simulation on the drawing

In E1, Alex simulates the open 2D space from the values in the model and shows each result as a Simulation results card with the method, the inputs, the assumptions, any warnings and the result tables.

For process engineers, a line whose line list has a composition, a pressure and a temperature gets a flash with the Peng-Robinson method: its phases, their amounts and compositions, density, Z, enthalpy, Cp and viscosity. When lines carry a composition, Alex solves the heat and material balance along the drawing through valves, pumps, compressors, heaters and coolers, exchangers, mixers, splitters and separators. Each unit needs its specification on its attributes; Alex asks for what is missing and never assumes it.

For electrical engineers, on a single line diagram, Alex works out load flow and the IEC 60909 short-circuit current at every board, motor starting, arc flash to IEEE 1584-2018, earth faults, harmonics to IEEE 519-2014, protection coordination from the relay, trip unit and fuse settings you entered, and battery sizing and UPS autonomy to IEEE 485 and IEEE 1115.

Every assumption a simulation makes is listed on its card, and a red Not converged says the numbers are not reliable. Export results (Excel) writes a summary sheet and one sheet per table. A calculated stream is written to the line list only when you press Write to the line list. Stream tables from HYSYS, Aspen Plus, DWSIM or a similar simulator are imported into the line list, matched to lines and checked by you.

### Animate flow: see what the plant does

In E1, one button sets a sheet in motion: on a PFD or P&ID the flow moves through the pipes the way it goes and as fast as it goes, tanks fill and empty and pumps turn.

Click a pump to stop it, or a valve to close it, and see what happens downstream. The lines after a stopped pump empty, the ones before it pulse as blocked, and a pump with a closed outlet valve is reported as dead-headed. A tank whose outlet is shut fills, with its level alarms LAH and LAHH, and a trend window draws every tank's level over the last ten minutes with the alarm limits.

Hold the pointer on a moving line to read its fluid, phase, flow, pressure, temperature, size, velocity, Reynolds number and friction loss. Color by → Velocity check colours lines green, amber or red against the usual velocity ranges and the erosional velocity of API RP 14E. On single line, circuit, wiring and loop diagrams, Animate current runs the current from the supply to the loads, checks cable loading against IEC 60364-5-52 ratings and voltage drop, and shows which motor loses its supply when a breaker opens.

Nothing in the model changes. Reset puts every valve, pump and switch back as drawn.

### Design validation: checks that run as you work

In E1, everything soft about an object is a finding with a severity, error, warning or information, listed on the object's Checks tab and for the whole project.

Findings come from a required value that is missing, a relationship minimum not reached, a tag that is pending or out of date, an object that breaks its class's behavior, a check rule your organization wrote, a calculation with a missing input, and the piping check. An open error blocks issuing a revision of a document that shows it, until it is fixed or accepted with a comment by a lead engineer.

Check piping… follows the flow through every pipe on a 2D space and finds a pump turned the wrong way, pipe that meets head-on and pipelines that are no longer whole. It offers fixes and never applies one on its own. For wiring, E1 runs the entity check of intrinsically safe loops and the voltage budget of each loop at 20 mA; a value it needs and does not have is reported as missing, never taken as zero.

Safety and progress are checked the same way. A safety instrumented function shows its PFD, achieved SIL and hardware fault tolerance against the required SIL. A workflow step can require values confirmed, no open errors or a revision issued before an item moves on.

### A full-context AI agent to pressure-test the design

In E1, when you ask Alex whether a design is right or complete, Alex's own review of the 2D space runs first, with your company's accepted conventions, and the answer is based on its findings.

Ask in the Agent tab, in Ask mode if you want answers only: “Is the design of this 2D space right? What is missing?” The answer cites what Alex observed and, where they apply, your company's conventions, with the clause they come from. The review changes nothing in the project.

Alex's checks cover line velocity, pressure drop, erosional velocity and design margin, sour service, instrument loops, fail positions, interlocks against the cause and effect matrix, and anti-surge. As HAZOP leader, Alex prepares a HAZOP worksheet from the drawing with nodes, deviations, causes, consequences, safeguards, a LOPA per scenario, the API 521 relief cases and the risk matrix, for your team to work through. See predictive engineering with Alex.

### Explore and compare design options

In E1, design options are kept side by side as cases, module variants or branches, and compared with what was issued.

A case is a variant of an object, for example another operating condition of a pump: it takes over the object's values until you type its own, so you only enter what differs. On a specification datasheet, the operating cases stand side by side. A module can have options and named variants, and a placed module switches to another variant.

For a larger alternative, make a branch of part of the design and change it while main stays as it is; push it back when it is ready, or close it. See branches and modifications.

To see what changed, Changes since… draws a cloud on a 2D space around everything added, deleted, modified or moved since a day, a revision or a version. The cause and effect matrix and the wiring are compared with an issued revision the same way.

- Simulation results with method, inputs and assumptions on every card
- Flow and current animated on the drawing, with nothing changed in the model
- Findings on every object, and a revision gate for open errors
- Cases, variants and branches to compare options

### Questions

**Does E1 replace a process simulator?** E1 flashes lines and solves a heat and material balance along the drawing, from the values in the model. For a rigorous process model, keep your simulator and import its stream table from HYSYS, Aspen Plus, DWSIM or similar into E1's line list.

**Does a simulation or the flow animation change my design?** No. Simulation results are cards, and the animation changes nothing in the model. A calculated value is written to the line list only when you press Write to the line list.

**What happens when data is missing?** Alex asks for what a simulation needs and lists every assumption it makes on the result card. The wiring checks report a missing value as missing, never as zero.

**Which electrical calculations are available?** On a single line diagram: load flow, IEC 60909 short circuit and earth faults, motor starting, IEEE 1584-2018 arc flash, IEEE 519-2014 harmonics, protection coordination, and IEEE 485 and IEEE 1115 battery and UPS sizing.

**Can a failed check stop a drawing from being issued?** Yes. While the project's revision gate is on, a revision is refused while the document shows an object with an open error. A lead engineer can accept the finding with a comment instead.

**How do I compare two design options?** Use cases for different operating conditions of one object, module variants for typical arrangements, and branches for a larger alternative. Changes since… shows what changed against a revision or a date.

## Work across disciplines on one project

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-multidiscipline-collaboration.html

In E1, process, instrumentation, electrical and automation engineers share one project and one plant data model. Each discipline works on the same objects at the same time and sees the others' changes within seconds, while the objects you are responsible for are changed only by you or your group.

### Multidiscipline engineering collaboration on one model

In E1, every discipline works in the same project, on the same objects, instead of exchanging files between separate tools.

A pump is one object in E1. The process engineer gives it its operating and design conditions, the instrumentation engineer the transmitter that measures it and its trips, the electrical engineer its motor and hazardous area, and the automation engineer the interlock in the cause and effect matrix. Each group of values is a section of the same datasheet, and every drawing, list and loop diagram reads the same object.

So there is no handover file to wait for and no copy to reconcile. When the process engineer renames a pump or changes a line, the wiring, the lists and every drawing of the pump show it at once. See one plant data model for how the model is built.

### Concurrent engineering, live

In E1, when several people have the same project open, each one sees the others' changes within seconds, without reloading.

The server pushes every change to everyone who has the project open: the explorer, the 2D spaces, the object windows and the lists. In our load tests a change reaches the rest of the team in about a second, with 50 engineers working at once on a project of 498,000 objects.

Avatars at the right of a 2D space's toolbar show who else has it open, with a pencil while they edit; a click lists each person with their role, Viewing or Editing, and since when. You never see anyone's pointer or unsaved work, and nothing about who opened what is recorded.

E1 saves each object on its own, so two engineers can work on the same drawing at the same time. If two people change the same object at the same moment, the first change is kept, the second is refused with a clear message, and the second person's copy is reloaded so they see the current state. Nothing is overwritten unseen.

### Keep ownership of your scope

In E1, one person or one group can be made responsible for an object, a folder, a sheet or a whole section, and only they then change it and everything in it.

On an object's page, Take it makes you responsible for something nobody owns yet, and a lead engineer uses Assign to… to give it to a person or a group, such as Mechanical. Everyone else still sees it and comments on it; a colleague who tries to change it is refused with your name and asked to contact you. Project settings → Access lists every responsibility with Release.

Permissions can follow the disciplines too. A custom role may change the attributes of one discipline only: process engineers a pump's process data, electrical engineers its motor and hazardous area data. The disciplines are process, mechanical, piping, electrical and instrumentation.

Roles are given on the organization, a project, a section or a single object. A project administrator can share one drawing with a subcontractor as Engineer, or mark a finished drawing as read-only by giving others Reviewer or Viewer on it.

### Discuss the design where it is

In E1, every object, project, folder and 2D space has a Chat tab where colleagues discuss it, with @mentions, #links to other objects, replies and resolved threads.

During a drawing review, pin a message right where the question is. The pin is numbered on the 2D space, and the object shows Needs review in the explorer until the message is resolved.

A task asks a person or a group to do something, with a type, a due date, a description, a screenshot and a checklist, once or repeating. The people it is for see it in their Inbox, together with the messages that mention them, and can choose which notices also come by email.

Automated assistants keep the other disciplines informed: when an object of a chosen class is renamed, a revision is rejected or an item moves to another workflow step, the people you chose are notified or given a task.

### Work apart, then bring it together with branches and review

In E1, a discipline can work on a branch of part of the design while main stays as it is, then push it back as one change after review.

Pull from main brings main's changes into the branch value by value; what both changed differently is a conflict you resolve, also on the drawing. A branch type can require a review before main, with four eyes: a colleague approves or requests changes, and the author does not approve their own branch. Every push leaves a protocol with who pushed and every field before and after.

Workflows add the sign-offs between disciplines. Each approval step, such as Checked or Approved, is signed by someone who did not move the item into it, and an item changed after its approval shows Changed since Approved. See branches and modifications, and projects across companies for an owner and its contractors on one shared project.

- Live changes for everyone in the project, about a second after they are saved
- Responsibility for objects, folders, sheets and sections
- Permissions per discipline's attributes
- Chat, pins, tasks and an Inbox on the objects themselves
- Branches with merge review and push protocols

### Questions

**Can two engineers work on the same P&ID at the same time?** Yes. E1 saves each object on its own and pushes every change to everyone who has the drawing open. Avatars on the toolbar show who else is viewing or editing it.

**What happens when two people change the same object?** The first change is kept. The second is refused with a clear message, and that person's copy is reloaded with the current state, so nothing is overwritten without anyone noticing.

**How do I stop others from changing my part of the design?** Take responsibility for the object, folder, sheet or section, or have a lead engineer assign it to your group. Only you or your group can then change it; everyone else can still see it and comment.

**Can electrical engineers change only electrical data?** Yes. A custom role can be limited to the attributes of one discipline, such as a pump's motor and hazardous area data, while the process data stays with the process engineers.

**How do we review another discipline's work?** Pin messages on the drawing, give tasks with a checklist, and use branches with a merge review before changes reach main. A workflow approval is signed by someone who did not move the item into that step.

**Can our contractors work in the same project?** Yes. A project can be shared with another organization: the owner company and its contractor work on the same project, each managing its own people and licenses.

## Built for refinery-size projects

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-large-projects.html

In E1, a project the size of a refinery stays fast for the whole team. E1 is load-tested every night and every week on a project with 498,000 objects, 1,300 dense sheets and 50 engineers working at once on one server: the project opens in under 2 seconds, a typical edit is saved in a few tenths of a second, and every change reaches the rest of the team in about a second.

### Large project performance, measured

In E1, performance is measured on a project the size of a refinery, not on a small sample.

The test project holds 498,000 objects: equipment, valves, instruments, lines, cables, wires, signals and ports, drawn on 1,300 dense sheets. It is the order of size of a grassroots refinery, a petrochemical complex or an offshore platform. E1 opens it, edits it and searches it on every nightly run.

For one engineer working on this project, these are the measured times. They are the times of the server answering, so they show what E1 itself costs, before your connection is added.

- Open the project: 140–180 ms.
- Open an object: 3 ms.
- Edit a value: 110–130 ms. Rename: 15 ms.
- Move a symbol on a dense P&ID: 290–380 ms.
- First page of a filtered list: 50 ms.
- Search by tag, name or value, across all projects: 10 ms.
- Errors in any run: 0.

### Deep view: find your way through a large model, object by object

Deep view shows an object and every object associated with it, as a data model of cards and links, like an object diagram rather than a drawing. You open it layer by layer with +1, or all at once with Expand all, until nothing more is linked.

On a large project, Expand all opens an object's whole network until it stops and says so; every kind of link has a chip with its count, and Find in view outlines the cards you are looking for.

Click a card to see its values and links, with Open, Show in tree and Deep view of this. Highlight route draws the way from one card to another in bold while everything else fades; Find in view outlines the cards whose tag, name, class or value holds your text; a chip for each kind of link shows or hides those links.

- Opened from the object window's Deep view tab, or from a symbol on a 2D space: right-click → Open ▸ Deep view.

### 50 engineers at once on one project

In E1, a whole project team works in the same project at the same time, and each engineer sees the others' changes without reloading.

The load test runs 50 engineers at once on the same 498,000-object project and records the slowest 5 % of every action (p95). With all 50 editing, opening the project takes 1.0–1.9 s, opening a drawing 0.9–1.8 s, editing a value 0.7–1.5 s and opening an object 300–500 ms. Late in a project most of the team only looks: with 45 engineers looking and 5 editing, opening the project takes 470 ms, a drawing 380 ms and an object 70 ms.

A change by one engineer reaches everyone who has the project open in about a second, pushed by the server, in the explorer, on 2D spaces, in object windows and in lists. Your own changes that are still being saved are kept while others' arrive.

E1 saves each object on its own, so engineers working on different symbols of one busy P&ID do not get in each other's way. When two people change the same object at the same moment, the first change is kept, the second is refused with a clear message, and that person's copy is reloaded so they see the current state.

### Dense P&IDs that open in the browser

In E1, a P&ID with thousands of symbols opens and responds in the browser in well under a second.

Large plants have large drawings. Measured in Chromium, a P&ID with 1,000 symbols opens in 260–320 ms and selects a symbol in 30 ms. A P&ID with 3,000 symbols opens in 530 ms and selects a symbol in 140–150 ms. Nothing needs to be split up or simplified to keep a sheet usable.

On a busy sheet several disciplines often work at once: a process engineer, an instrument engineer and a checker. Avatars at the right of a 2D space's toolbar show who else has it open, with a pencil while they edit, so you know who is changing what. E1 never shows anyone's pointer or unsaved work, and records nothing about who opened what.

### Finding your way through 500,000 objects

In E1, the explorer, the search and the lists are built so that a large project stays easy to read and quick to change in bulk.

The explorer search filters the tree as you type and finds objects by tag, name, line number or any value, also as a quantity: 24 volt finds every value of 24 V in any unit. Projects lists every project you can see, and the explorer shows only the ones you add, so the tree stays short. Up to five columns beside each name, such as class, status or any attribute, make the explorer read as a tree and a table, and folders a team does not use can be hidden.

Lists are live queries of the model. Filter them with AND, OR and NOT, group them with totals, and run one query over every project of your organization. Work in bulk as in Excel: paste a block copied from Excel with a preview of every change first, give many cells one value with Set value…, fill down, and undo it as one step. Every query exports to Excel, CSV or JSON and reads back with Update from Excel….

Existing projects come in at scale. Import Excel tag lists and data sheets, DEXPI P&IDs, and P&IDs from CAD as DXF or as PDF; import again later to update what is there, deciding every difference yourself.

### Clear scopes in a big team

In E1, each engineer and each group keeps ownership of their scope while the whole team works in one project.

Project roles go from Viewer and Reviewer to Engineer, Lead engineer and Project administrator, given to people or to groups. With Assign to…, one person or group becomes responsible for an object, a folder, a sheet or a whole section: only they change it and everything in it, while everyone else still views and comments. A custom role can change the attributes of one discipline only, so electrical engineers edit a pump's motor data and process engineers its process data.

Dashboards show where a large project stands: Project progress, Data completeness, Review and comments and Branches are there from the start, and trends such as the S-curve show progress by week against the plan. Click a number or a bar to list the items behind it.

### Tested every night against fixed budgets

In E1, performance is part of every build: a change that makes E1 slower fails before it reaches a customer.

Every change to E1 is timed against fixed budgets, and a slower build fails. Every week a stress test runs 100 engineers at once, twice the design load of 50, and a one-hour soak test checks that E1 stays fast over time.

In the E1 Cloud, the E1 server adds capacity when it is busy and is always running, so there is no cold start. Health checks every few seconds replace a server that stops answering. The figures on this page are measured in our load tests; times in the E1 Cloud depend on the size of your project, how many people work at once and your connection. The full results are in the cloud specifications.

### Questions

**How large a project can E1 handle?** E1 is tested every night on a project with 498,000 objects and 1,300 dense sheets, with 50 engineers working at once, and every week with 100 engineers at once. That is the size of a refinery, a petrochemical complex or an offshore platform.

**How fast does a large project open?** For one engineer, the 498,000-object test project opens in 140–180 ms on the server. With 50 engineers all editing at once, the slowest 5 % of openings take 1.0–1.9 s.

**Do engineers see each other's changes?** Yes. A change by one engineer reaches everyone who has the project open in about a second, pushed by the server, without reloading.

**What happens when two engineers change the same object?** E1 saves each object on its own. The first change is kept, the second is refused with a clear message, and the second person's copy is reloaded so they see the current state.

**Can I search across all my projects?** Yes. The search finds objects by tag, name or any value, also as a quantity such as 24 volt, across all your projects; on the test project it answers in about 10 ms. A query can also list the objects of every project of your organization.

**Are these times guaranteed in the E1 Cloud?** They are measured in our load tests. Times in the E1 Cloud depend on the size of your project, how many people work at once and your connection. See the cloud specifications for the full results.

**How do I bring an existing large project into E1?** Import Excel tag lists and data sheets, DEXPI P&IDs, and P&IDs from CAD as DXF or PDF. Each import can be run again later to update what is there, and you decide every difference.

## Across companies on one project

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-cross-company-projects.html

In E1, an owner company, its EPC contractor and specialist firms work in the same live project instead of emailing the latest ZIP. The project stays with the organization that shares it; each other organization chooses its own people, uses its own licenses, and works up to the highest role the sharing organization allows.

### Share a live project with another organization

In E1, a Project administrator shares a project with another organization, and that organization's administrator decides which of its own people work on it.

Owner-operator and EPC collaboration usually means copies: a model exported, zipped, emailed, changed and sent back, with nobody quite sure which file is current. In E1 there is one project. The client, the contractor and the specialists open the same objects, drawings, lists and documents, and see each other's changes within seconds.

Sharing takes two steps. In the project's Project settings → Access, the Project administrator chooses the highest role the other organization may give, for example at most Engineer, and clicks Share with another organization…. E1 shows a code once, valid for 14 days, to send to the other organization's administrator. There, under File → Organization… → Shared projects, the Owner or an Administrator enters the code, clicks Accept and gives each of their members a role on the project.

Their members then switch to the sharing organization and work on that project only. History shows their organization after their name, so every change says which company made it. Either side clicks End to stop: the other organization's people lose the project at once.

### Clear boundaries between companies

In E1, the people of a partner organization are guests: they work within the role you allow and manage nothing of yours.

Whatever role a guest holds on the shared project, they manage nothing in your organization and have no integration access. The highest role you set when sharing caps what their administrator can give. The project roles are Viewer (views and exports), Reviewer (views and comments), Engineer (creates and edits objects, attributes, relations and drawings), Lead engineer (also issues revisions and approves branches) and Project administrator.

Inside the project, scopes are as clear as between disciplines.
