With Assign to…, a contractor's group becomes responsible for a section, a folder, a sheet or an object: only that group changes it, while everyone else views and comments. A responsibility never gives anyone a permission they do not have, and the same rule holds for Alex, imports and the API. Custom roles can limit a firm to one discipline's attributes, such as electrical or instrumentation.

A contractor's people use their own organization's licenses, not your seats. Guests invited to a project to view, such as clients and contractors, view for free.

### Decide what reviewers and viewers see

In E1, everything in a project is open to its members until you hide it: a whole project from viewers, or one attribute on a class or on one object.

Reviewers and viewers are often people outside your company: the client, a contractor, an inspector. A person with a Reviewer license is in the built-in group Reviewers, one with a Viewer license in Viewers, and you can tick anyone else into these groups, for example a contractor with an Editor license, so they see only what that group sees.

Set a project's Visible to so that viewers do not see it at all. Mark an attribute Editors only on a class, so that no reviewer or viewer sees, for example, the flow rate of any pump. Hide one value from viewers on one object. Hidden values are left out on the server, so they are missing everywhere for that circle: the object page, lists and their Excel exports, datasheets and their PDFs, history, Alex's context and the API.

### One record instead of the latest ZIP

In E1, questions, tasks and decisions between companies are kept on the objects they are about.

Discuss an object on its Chat tab: @mention a colleague from either company, #link another object, reply and resolve. Give a person or a group a task with a type, a due date and a screenshot; they find it in their Inbox and mark it done. Keep PDFs, spreadsheets and drawings with an object or the project as attachments.

Deliverables between owner and contractor go through E1's document control: each revision is signed along its purpose's route and issued as a PDF that never changes, with what changed since the revision before (see revisions, datasheets and reports). Larger changes can be prepared in a branch and reviewed before they reach main (see branches).

### Every step on the record

In E1, sharing a project, accepting it, giving roles and ending it are written to the audit logs of both organizations.

Owners and Administrators see every change to members, licenses, groups, roles and responsibilities with its before and after, see who had access on any earlier date, and export the history to Excel or CSV for an audit. An access review sends a project's access to a reviewer, who keeps or removes each line.

Where a company's privacy rules do not allow names, Configuration → Privacy makes history show only the groups people are in. E1 support has no access to your data. More on protection and data location is on the security page.

### Questions

**Who owns a project that is shared with another company?** The organization that shares it. The other organization's people work on it as guests, and the project stays with you when the sharing ends.

**Does a contractor use our licenses?** No. The other organization's people use their own licenses, not your seats. Guests invited to view a project, such as clients and contractors, view for free.

**How does the other company join the project?** Your Project administrator clicks Share with another organization… in the project's Access settings and sends the code, valid for 14 days. Their Owner or Administrator accepts it under File → Organization… → Shared projects and chooses their people and roles.

**Can a contractor see everything in our project?** Only what you leave open. Hide a project from viewers, an attribute on a class from reviewers and viewers, or one value on one object. Hidden values are left out on the server, also in exports, PDFs, history and the API.

**Can a contractor administer our organization?** No. Guests manage nothing and have no integration access, whatever role they hold on the project, and their roles are capped by the highest role you allowed.

**How do we stop sharing?** Either organization clicks End. The other organization's people lose the project at once, and the step is in both audit logs.

## Branches for scenarios and modifications

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-branches-modifications.html

In E1, a branch is a working copy of part of a project's design. Engineers change it while main stays as it is, pull main's changes in value by value, resolve conflicts on the data and on the drawing, and push the branch back to main as one change that undoes as one. Use branches for what-ifs, design changes, modification packages and commissioning scopes.

### Change part of the design while main stays as it is

In E1, a branch holds a chosen scope of the plant model; what you change in it changes the branch, not the project's main design.

Start a branch from the project's Branches page, from the project's right-click menu, or by selecting objects in the explorer or on a 2D space and choosing Branch ▸ New branch…. A scope preview lists what comes with your choice and why: a pump brings its nozzles, its connected lines and the 2D space it is drawn on as Editable, and its owner as Information. Change a row to Leave out or Information where it is not locked, and create the branch.

Enter the branch and the whole project shows the branch's content, with a bar that says you are in it. The branch icon marks every object and 2D space it changes. Objects outside the branch are grey and cannot be changed there. On a drawing, Show main lays main's current version on top in pink, so you see exactly what the branch draws differently, and Branches on this drawing shows every open branch that changes a 2D space, each in its colour.

Some things always belong to main: issuing a revision, the project's settings and the library are refused in a branch. Tag numbers are taken centrally, so two branches never give the same number. A branch never widens what you may change in main.

### Pull from main and resolve conflicts, value by value

In E1, Pull from main brings main's changes into a branch value by value; only what both sides changed differently is a conflict.

When someone changes main in the branch's scope, a bell rings on the branch's card and lists what changed and who changed it. Pull from main takes everything main changed that the branch did not. A value both changed differently is listed under Conflicts, grouped by object, with Base, Main and Branch side by side: choose Keep mine, Take theirs, or type a value and Use value. Keep mine everywhere and Take theirs everywhere settle many at once.

Conflicts are resolved on the drawing too. A symbol both sides moved shows twice, Main in blue and Branch in orange, joined by a dashed line: click the one to keep. Statuses follow the same rule: where main and the branch both changed a status, E1 proposes the lower one, and a signature given in a branch is void after a later change there.

### Review before main: branch types and merge requests

In E1, each branch has a type that says whether it needs a review before it reaches main, and how its conflicts and main's edits are handled.

Every project starts with three branch types: Working branch, Design change (reviewed) and Commissioning package. A Project administrator sets for each type Review before main, Four eyes, what happens After push, how Editing in main treats the branch's objects (Mark, Warn or Block) and a rule for graphical conflicts. A tag or validation conflict is always a person's choice.

A branch that needs a review asks for one with Ask for review. The reviewers find the merge request in their Inbox, and the objects show Under merge review meanwhile. A Lead engineer approves or clicks Request changes… with what should change; with four eyes the author cannot approve their own branch. Alex never approves or rejects a merge request: a person does.

For plants that run a management of change (MOC) process, a reviewed branch keeps each modification separate from the design of record until a second engineer has approved it, and leaves a protocol of everything it changed. The MOC procedure itself stays your company's.

### Push to main as one change, with a protocol

In E1, Push to main brings a branch into the project as one change, and every push leaves a protocol of what it changed.

A Lead engineer or above pushes, and their role must allow every change in the branch. E1 refuses a push while main has changes in the branch's scope that were not pulled yet, while conflicts are open, or while a required review is not approved, so nothing in main is overwritten unseen. The push lands as one change, Pushed branch…, in main's history, and Undo this change takes it all back.

Every push of a branch or a commissioning package writes a push protocol: its date, who pushed, and every object it created, changed or deleted, with each field before and after. A protocol is written by the push itself and never changes. After the push, the branch stays open and counts from what it pushed, or closes when its type says so.

### Commissioning packages cut from a branch

In E1, finished parts of a branch become commissioning packages that go to main on their own, each with its dates, lead and description.

On a branch's card, New commissioning package makes a package. Inside the branch, draw around the work on a drawing with Package boundary (lasso, rectangle or ellipse) and add it, or right-click objects and choose Branch ▸ Add to commissioning package. A pipe that leaves the boundary is marked where it crosses it, and the package lists what it still needs, such as an area the branch created.

Give the package its description, priority, planned commissioning date, commissioning lead and who accepts it. Mark ready cuts it from the branch as it is, then it is reviewed and pushed to main alone. The branch then counts from main for those objects, so its next pull has no conflict and its push does not repeat them. Set Commissioned on once the plant it holds is commissioned. Branches and packages are objects of the library classes Branch and Commissioning package, so they carry your own attributes and appear in queries.

### Branches on the dashboard, and Alex in a branch

In E1, the Branches dashboard and each object's Branches tab show what is being changed where.

Dashboards → Branches shows open branches, those in review, their average age, open conflicts and branches by status and owner. An object's Branches tab lists the open branches that may change it, with what each has changed so far. Owners, an owner group and an assignee make clear who is responsible for each branch, and Access and sharing can limit a branch to the people who should see it.

In a branch, Alex and stored assistants change the branch, never main, and only what you may change. A change Alex proposes can be kept as a branch with Open as branch, to review it before anything reaches the design of record.

### Questions

**What is a branch in E1?** A working copy of part of a project's design. You change it while main stays as it is, pull main's changes in, and push it back to main as one change when it is ready.

**What can I use branches for?** What-if scenarios, design changes that need a review, modification packages and commissioning scopes. Each project starts with the branch types Working branch, Design change (reviewed) and Commissioning package.

**What happens when main and a branch change the same value?** Pull from main lists it as a conflict with Base, Main and Branch side by side. You choose Keep mine, Take theirs or type a value. A symbol both moved is shown twice on the drawing so you can click the one to keep.

**Who can push a branch to main?** A Lead engineer or above, whose role allows every change in the branch. A push is refused while main has unpulled changes in its scope, while conflicts are open, or while a required review is not approved.

**Can I undo a push?** Yes. A push lands in main's history as one change, and Undo this change takes it all back. Its push protocol keeps every change it made, each field before and after.

**Can I issue a revision inside a branch?** No. Issuing revisions, the project's settings and the library are changed in main. Push the branch first, then issue the revision there.

**What is a commissioning package?** A part of a branch collected by drawing around it or by right-click, with its dates, lead and description. Once marked ready and reviewed, it is pushed to main on its own.

## Revisions, datasheets and reports

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-revisions-datasheets-reports.html

In E1, engineering documents are made from the live model: lists, reports, datasheets and drawings print from the same data the engineers edit. Each revision is frozen when it is created, signed along its purpose's route, and issued as a PDF that never changes, with clouds and a table of what changed since the revision before.

### Engineering documents generated from the model

In E1, every document of a project is in its Documents section, and most of them are generated from the model rather than drawn by hand.

New document… makes a document by choosing its kind. A list document shows a saved query and prints it to PDF and Excel with a title block. A plot prints a 2D space on a chosen page format with chosen layers. A datasheet document puts an object's datasheet under revision control. Reports, PDF packages and the project's deliverables set bind several of them together.

Documents made elsewhere have their place too. An uploaded document keeps a PDF from outside and revises it like any other. A hyperlink stands for a file kept in your engineering document management system: it opens the file there, and any object can be documented by it, so the file is found from the pump or the area it is about.

The document number is the document's tag, made by the project's tag rules; a 2D space gets its number from a pattern such as {project.code}-{docType}-{seq:4}, giving P-PID-0001. The All ▾ filter shows only the drawings, the lists, the datasheets or the hyperlinks.

### Revision control with purposes of issue and sign-off

In E1, a revision freezes what a document shows when it is created, goes through sign-off, and is issued as a filed PDF that never changes.

Create revision… asks for a purpose of issue, such as IFR — Issued for review or IFC — Issued for construction, and gives the next label of the project's revision scheme. By default the labels are A, B, C … skipping I, O, Q, S, X and Z, then 0, 1, 2 … from construction. A project can instead use ISO 19650 (P01 … then C01 …), numeric labels, letters only, or the company's own scheme, and EPC purposes of issue or ISO 19650 suitability codes.

Every revision is signed along its purpose's route: by who prepared it, checked by someone else, and approved by someone with Issue revisions, a Lead engineer or above. Each signature names what is signed and may ask you to confirm it is you. A Reviewer, an access token and Alex never sign. Reject… and Withdraw… take a revision back, and Reassign… gives a step to another signer; a step past its days to sign is marked Late.

The last signature issues the revision: its PDF is made once, filed under Documents, and stays byte for byte as issued, even after the model changes. The revision before is superseded. While the revision gate is on, an open error on what the document shows refuses the revision, so a known problem is fixed or accepted before it is issued. Internal versions, such as C.1 after Rev B, are printed INTERNAL — NOT FOR ISSUE.

### Clouds and change tables in every revision

In E1, each revision is compared with the one before it, and its PDF shows what changed.

On a drawing's revision, the PDF draws a cloud around each change with a triangle carrying the revision label, and lists every change beside the title block, for example a design pressure from 16 bar(g) to 25 bar(g). The comparison is frozen when the output is created, so a later edit never changes an issued PDF. Compare with… lists the changes between any two outputs of a document.

Between revisions, the document lists what changed since the last issue, and the explorer marks each modified or added object. Changes since… on a 2D space clouds everything added, deleted, modified or moved since a day, a revision or a version, with before → after and who changed it.

### Instrument and equipment datasheets

In E1, an object's datasheet is the screen its values are viewed and edited on and the page that prints, so the datasheet and the model never disagree.

Specification datasheets have numbered lines, tables of parts that continue on continuation pages, operating cases side by side, and revision marks, the same on screen and in the PDF. Type values straight into the datasheet; units are added and checked, and Undo takes a change back. After a datasheet document is issued, each value changed since shows the next revision beside it.

Ready-made templates cover instruments, valves, pumps and exchangers. They are E1's own templates inspired by ISA, API and ASME specification datasheets: only the idea comes from those forms, and the layout, wording and line numbers are E1's. Copy one to edit it in the datasheet designer, or build your own layout from components.

One datasheet document can cover several tags of one class: shared values are shown once, differing ones read See list, and one change sets them all. Issuing its revision records every tag.

### Reports, PDF packages and the deliverables set

In E1, reports and document sets are bound from saved queries and issued documents, and revised like any single document.

Add to report… on a saved query makes a report or adds the query as a section of one. Its PDF prints every section under its heading, grouped by a column such as Area, with the header on every page and page numbers; Export Excel writes a sheet per section. A list's Excel export reads back with Update from Excel…, which lists every change before it is applied.

A PDF package binds up to 1,000 documents into one PDF with a cover and an index, taking each document's current revision; a revision of the package holds issued revisions only. Documents → Deliverables binds the project's drawings with its reports and datasheets into one PDF with a cover, an index and page numbers, previews it marked DRAFT, and issues it with a purpose of issue.

### An audit trail for every document

In E1, every version and revision of a document keeps a complete record of who created, signed, issued, withdrew or deleted it.

Audit report (CSV) and Audit report (PDF) list each event in time order: created, signed with the sentence signed and the sign-in, rejected, issued with the PDF's SHA-256 fingerprint, withdrawn, deleted and restored with their reasons. Delete… with a reason takes an output out of a document, but a record stays, its label is never used again, and Restore brings it back for the project's kept period, 30 days by default.

Project settings → Documents chooses the revision scheme, the number pattern, the purposes of issue, the sign-off route of each purpose, four-eyes, the filing rule for issued PDFs and who sees versions. Each setting applies to outputs made afterwards; outputs already made never change.

### Questions

**Which revision schemes does E1 support?** Letters before construction and numbers from construction (the default), ISO 19650 (P01 … then C01 …), numeric labels, letters only, or your company's and project's own schemes, chosen in Project settings → Documents.

**Who can sign and issue a revision?** Checking needs Sign revisions (Engineer and above); approving and issuing need Issue revisions (Lead engineer and above). Someone else checks and approves unless a small team turns four-eyes off. A Reviewer, an access token and Alex never sign.

**Does an issued PDF ever change?** No. An issued revision's PDF is made once, filed, and stays byte for byte as issued, even after the model changes. Its snapshot, signatures and PDF cannot be changed from any surface.

**How do I see what changed since the last revision?** A drawing's revision PDF clouds each change and lists it beside the title block. Compare with… lists the changes between any two outputs, and the explorer marks objects modified or added since the last issue.

**Are the datasheet templates ISA or API forms?** No. They are E1's own templates inspired by ISA, API and ASME specification datasheets, for instruments, valves, pumps and exchangers. No form name, number, logo or wording of theirs is used.

**Can E1 keep documents made outside E1?** Yes. An uploaded document keeps a PDF from outside and revises it, and a hyperlink stands for a file kept in your document management system and opens it there.

**Can I get lists and reports in Excel?** Yes. List documents and reports export to PDF and Excel, and an exported list reads back with Update from Excel…, which checks every change before it is applied.

## Brownfield engineering and plant modifications, on the plant you already have

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-maintenance-brownfield.html

In E1, an existing plant is not a special case. You bring its P&IDs and lists in from CAD, PDF, DEXPI and Excel, record what is installed as as-built, change it in a modification branch while the shared design stays untouched, and hand the field a list of exactly what to lift and land. Every change is recorded, compared and can be undone.

### Start from the drawings you already have

In E1, legacy P&IDs become real objects: File → Import ▸ Legacy diagrams reads DXF and vector PDF drawings, and File → Import reads DEXPI 2.0 files and Excel workbooks.

Most brownfield plants were drawn in AutoCAD or a similar CAD program. E1 reads the drawings saved as DXF. Each block, such as a pump, a valve or a tank, becomes an object of the class it is named for or looks like, placed where it is drawn, and the lines on each layer become pipes, signals or cables connected to the symbols they end on. A DWG file is opened in your CAD program and saved as DXF first; E1 recognizes a DWG file and says so.

Often the only copy of a P&ID is a PDF. When it was exported from CAD, E1 finds the symbols among the lines, groups the ones drawn alike, recognizes each group against E1's symbols, takes the text beside a symbol as its tag and makes a pipeline from each line number. Import all sheets of a set together, so a tag drawn on two sheets is one object. A scanned image cannot be read, and E1 says so.

Every import proposes a class for each kind of thing with a confidence and a reason, shows every change before anything is stored, and takes it all back with one Ctrl+Z. Import a revised drawing or workbook again and the objects already there are updated, never duplicated. A value someone changed in E1 is never overwritten without your decision: you choose Use file or Keep E1.

- DXF drawings from AutoCAD and other CAD programs, up to 50 MB each.
- Vector PDF drawings, up to 50 MB and 50 pages per file.
- DEXPI 2.0 P&IDs from other P&ID tools, with their drawing kept as the background.
- Excel workbooks and CSV: equipment lists and instrument indexes, one class per sheet, one attribute per column.

### Record what is installed, as-built

In E1, every landed core and every terminal carries a construction status: Designed, Issued for construction, Installed, Terminated, Loop-checked, As-built or To be removed.

The wiring of an existing plant, or of a vendor's panel, comes into E1 as a termination list in CSV or Excel. Alex shows first what it would do, then makes the enclosures, strips, terminals, cables and cores that are not yet in the project. Every core is landed at both ends, fixed, with the scope Existing and the status As-built, so new design is made around it and E1 never moves it by itself.

Documents stay where they are when that suits you. A hyperlink in E1 stands for one file kept in your document management system and opens it there; relate it to a pump, a motor, a system or a 2D space and the file is found from that object. A PDF made elsewhere can be kept as an uploaded document with its own revisions.

Reviewers confirm the drawing against the plant with the project's markup stamps. Field verified and As-built are among the stamps a project starts with, and each stamp carries the reviewer's name and the date.

### Plant modifications in a branch, not in the live design

In E1, a modification is a branch of part of the design: you change it while main stays as it is, and push it back as one change when it is ready.

Start a branch from the objects the modification touches, on the drawing or in the explorer. E1 adds what comes with them, such as nozzles and connected lines, and explains why. Inside the branch, Show main lays main's version of the 2D space over yours, so you see exactly what moves. When main changes an object the branch may change, the branch is told, and Pull from main brings the change in value by value, with any conflict for a person to resolve.

Finished work can be cut out as a commissioning package: draw around the equipment, give the package its dates and commissioning lead, mark it ready, and push only that part. A branch type can require a review by a colleague before main. Every push leaves a protocol with every field before and after. Branches are described in full on Branches and modifications.

### Changes after issue: a wire move list for the field

In E1, issued wiring is never moved silently: once cables are pulled and terminated, a change becomes a list of what to lift and what to land, terminal by terminal.

Move a transmitter to another junction box and E1 writes the moves on the Changes tab of the Wiring page: Lift, Land or Remove, with the core, its wire number, the terminal and the reason. A device whose wiring is installed cannot simply be deleted; it is marked to be removed first, and its connections are on the list.

The field view shows the moves in large rows by enclosure and strip, easy to hit with a finger on a tablet. One tap ticks a move off with your name and the time, and a comment goes back to design on the terminal. The move list also exports to Excel. Compare with shows what was added, removed and changed since an issued revision of the loop diagrams, or since a date.

### Redlining and change clouds on the drawing

In E1, redlines go on a Markups layer that never changes the drawing, and every markup has a card with its discussion and its status.

Reviewers mark up a 2D space with clouds, arrows, text, pins and stamps; a Reviewer can mark up but never change the drawing. A markup is accepted, rejected, answered or incorporated, and incorporating it names the changes that did it. A marked-up print carries each markup as a real PDF comment, and a reviewer's annotated copy of that print reads back into the review round. The Markups list exports the comment resolution sheet.

Changes since… on a 2D space clouds everything added, deleted, modified or moved since a day, a revision or a version, with before and after and who changed it. A revision's PDF clouds what changed with a triangle carrying its label and lists each change beside the title block. Each object's History tab shows when, who and what changed, and Undo this change takes one back.

### Questions

**Can E1 import DWG files?** E1 reads DXF. Open the DWG in your CAD program, use Save As → DXF, and import that file with File → Import ▸ Legacy diagrams ▸ DXF drawing…. E1 recognizes a DWG file and tells you to save it as DXF.

**Can E1 read a scanned P&ID?** No. E1 reads PDFs exported from a CAD program (vector PDFs). A scanned drawing is an image; E1 says so and imports nothing.

**What happens when I import a revised drawing?** Objects already in the project are found by their tag and updated, never duplicated. A value someone changed in E1 is shown beside the file's value, and you choose Use file or Keep E1 before Apply. A moved symbol is a placement for you to decide too.

**How many legacy drawings may we import?** Each organization may import 100 DXF and 100 PDF drawings on the University, Essentials and Standard plans, and any number on Enterprise. A file counts once per project, so a revised version uses nothing more. Excel and DEXPI imports have no limit. See Plans and prices.

**Which plans include modification branches?** Modification branches and commissioning packages are in the University, Standard (Editor) and Enterprise plans. Essentials (Editor Basic) has DXF and Excel import, redlining and document control, but not branches, PDF or DEXPI import.

**Does a redline change the drawing?** No. Markups are on their own Markups layer. They never change the drawing, its objects, their history or their revisions; hiding the layer shows the drawing unchanged.

**Can the field tick off wiring changes on a tablet?** Yes. On the Wiring page, Changes → Field view shows the wire moves in large rows for a finger. One tap marks a move done with your name and the time, and a comment goes back to design on the terminal.

## Maintenance and commissioning, on the live plant model

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-maintenance-commissioning.html

In E1, the plant you maintain and commission is the same model the engineers designed. Open any object and see everything linked to it, mark up the live diagrams in the office or on site, raise a technical or engineering query where the question is, talk about an object on the object itself, and collect finished work into a commissioning package.

### Modifications and commissioning packages in branches

In E1, a plant modification is made in a branch while the shared design stays untouched, and finished work is collected into a commissioning package.

Collect finished work into a commissioning package by drawing around it or by right-click, give it its dates, lead and description, then mark it ready and push it to main on its own. Every change is recorded and compared before it lands.

### Deep view: everything linked to an object, at a glance

Deep view shows an object and every object associated with it, as a data model of cards and links, like an object diagram rather than a drawing. You open it layer by layer with +1, or all at once with Expand all, until nothing more is linked.

From a valve you follow the pipes on its ports to the pump beyond, the transmitter that measures the pump, its terminals, the cable core landed on them, the cable and the junction box at its other end. Before you isolate, replace or test something, you see what it touches.

Click a card to see its values and links, with Open, Show in tree and Deep view of this. Highlight route draws the way from one card to another in bold while everything else fades; Find in view outlines the cards whose tag, name, class or value holds your text; a chip for each kind of link shows or hides those links.

- Opened from the object window's Deep view tab, or from a symbol on a 2D space: right-click → Open ▸ Deep view.
- The bar under the view counts the objects, links and levels shown, and the cards that have more to show.

### Redlining on the live diagrams

In E1, you mark up a 2D space with clouds, arrows, text, pins and stamps on a Markups layer that never changes the drawing, and each markup is discussed in its own card.

Every markup has a status and a response: accept, reject, answer, incorporate or close. Each change is written in its discussion and tells its author, so nothing raised on site is lost on the way back to the office.

The Markups list filters a 2D space's markups and runs a review round with its reviewers; when it is closed, the comment resolution sheet is exported. A marked-up print carries each markup as a real PDF comment, and a reviewer's annotated PDF reads back into E1 as markups in the round.

### On site with the iPad and the phone

E1 Reviewer for iPad and E1 Mobile for iPhone and Android launch with E1 on 19 May 2027, on the same model.

On the iPad, every drawing goes to site. Redline it with a pen, a cloud, an arrow, text or a stamp; each mark says what it means and carries a note, goes into a review round and is answered by the engineers in E1. Tap a symbol, a pipe, a signal or a cable to see its object: its properties, every attribute, its history and its chat.

On the phone, messages, tasks and Alex are in your pocket, typed or spoken. Everything lands in the same E1 model at once.

### Tasks, technical queries and engineering queries

In E1, a question about the plant is a task for a person or a group, not an e-mail.

New task… offers E1's seven task types, including Technical query and Engineering query, and your organization's own, each a task or a query. A task has a type, a due date, a description and a screenshot, once or repeating; the people it is for see it in their Inbox and mark it done.

A task can carry a checklist of items to tick, in the Inbox in E1 and the same in E1 Reviewer on the iPad.

### A chat on every object

In E1, every object has a Chat tab: the conversation about a pump, a valve or a cable stays with that pump, valve or cable.

@mention a colleague to bring them in, #link another object, reply, like, edit, delete and resolve. Whoever opens the object later reads why it is the way it is.

### Questions

**What is Deep view in E1?** Deep view shows an object and every object associated with it as cards and links. You open it layer by layer or all at once, highlight the route between two objects and find any object in the view.

**Can I raise a technical query in E1?** Yes. New task… offers Technical query and Engineering query among E1's seven task types, and your organization can add its own.

**Can I redline drawings on site?** Yes. In E1 you mark up any 2D space on a Markups layer, and E1 Reviewer for iPad, launching on 19 May 2027, redlines on site with the marks answered by the engineers in E1.

## Cloud plant engineering software, with nothing to install on servers

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-cloud-workspace.html

E1 Cloud is LANXTOR's software as a service for plant engineering. Your organization's projects, data and team are in one place at app.lanxtor.com, hosted on Microsoft Azure in the European Union. You create an account, invite your colleagues and start engineering the same day, in the browser or in the desktop app. LANXTOR runs the servers, the backups and the updates.

### Sign in, open the plant, keep going

In E1 Cloud, you open app.lanxtor.com in the browser or start the desktop app, sign in, and your projects are there. Nothing is installed on a server.

You sign in with your E1 account or with your company's Microsoft account. The first sign-in creates your account. A passkey signs you in with your screen lock or a security key, and Owners and Administrators need one before their rights take effect. A sign-in lasts 12 hours.

Your changes are saved on the server as you make them, and your tabs, selection and open rows come back after a reload. The status bar names where your projects are kept; on E1 Cloud it reads Microsoft Azure. E1 Cloud is always on the latest version of E1: when the server is updated, a bar tells you a new version is ready and you choose when to restart into it.

To try it, start a free 30-day trial: an organization of your own with 5 Editors, 5 Reviewers and unlimited Viewers invited as guests. The sample project Sample E1 gives you a complete fictional plant to explore. After a trial the organization is read-only for 90 more days, and everything can still be viewed and exported.

### Projects, data and teams in one organization

In E1, everything belongs to an organization: its members, their licenses, its projects and its company library. The plan and the invoice belong to the organization too.

Owners and Administrators invite colleagues by email with a license, or many at once from Excel. Each person has one license, Editor, Reviewer or Viewer, which caps what their roles may do. Roles are given on the organization, on a project, on a section or on a single object, to a person or to a group, and an organization can make roles of its own.

Projects are arranged in the explorer, and one query can run over the objects of every project you may view. Contractors and clients work on a shared project with their own people and licenses, up to the role you allow. Guests invited to a project view it for free.

### Work on the same plant at the same time

In E1 Cloud, several engineers work on one project at once and see each other's changes within seconds, pushed by the server, without reloading.

Avatars on a 2D space's toolbar show who else has it open and who is editing. When two people change the same thing, the first change is kept and the second is refused with a clear message, so nothing is overwritten unseen. Every object keeps its history, with who changed what, before and after.

Conversations stay with the work: comment on an object with mentions and replies, pin a message on a drawing, and give someone a task. The Inbox collects your mentions, replies and tasks, and you choose which notices come by email. Alex, the AI co-engineer, works in the same projects with your permissions and never more.

### Where your data is, and how it is protected

E1 Cloud runs in one Microsoft Azure region in the European Union, North Europe in Ireland. Your projects, drawings, documents and their backups stay in Azure data centres in the EU.

Every record in the database belongs to one organization, and PostgreSQL row-level security lets E1 read only the rows of the organization you work in. The database has no public address. Traffic is HTTPS only, and the database, files and backups are encrypted at rest with AES-256. E1 keeps no passwords.

The database can be restored to any minute of the last 7 days, and deleted files can be brought back for 14 days. Files are stored in three separate data centres of the region, and issued revisions are never removed. Owners and Administrators export the whole organization at any time, as open JSON lines and the original files. The full details are on E1 Cloud specifications.

- Region: EU, Microsoft Azure North Europe (Ireland); a US region, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud are coming.
- Recovery: at most 1 hour of work lost (RPO), service restored within 8 hours (RTO).
- Audit: sign-ins, members, licenses, roles and exports are recorded for administrators.
- Support: LANXTOR support sees account and billing data, not your projects, drawings or documents.

### Pay per user, per month

E1 Cloud is licensed per user and per month, with updates included. The plan belongs to the organization: up to 20 Editors on Essentials or Standard, and more on Enterprise.

Editors build the design, Reviewers review and approve, and Viewers see everything in E1 itself, read-only, not a PDF. AI credits are shared by the organization; more can be bought in packs, or your organization can use its own model key. Prices, plans and what each includes are on Plans and prices.

If your data must stay in your own cloud subscription or data centre, the same E1 runs as an enterprise installation.

### Questions

**What is E1 Cloud?** E1 Cloud is LANXTOR's hosted E1 at app.lanxtor.com: plant engineering software as a service. LANXTOR runs the servers, backups and updates on Microsoft Azure in the EU; you sign in and work in the browser or the desktop app.

**Where is our data stored?** In Microsoft Azure's North Europe region in Ireland. Database backups have a second copy in Azure's paired EU region, West Europe (the Netherlands). Projects, files and backups stay in the EU.

**Do we need to install anything?** No. E1 runs in the browser with nothing to install. The desktop app for Windows and macOS is optional and connects to E1 Cloud with one click: Use E1 Cloud.

**How do updates work?** E1 Cloud is always on the latest version, with updates included. When the server is updated, an open E1 tells you a new version is ready; Restart now opens it, and your work is already saved on the server.

**Can LANXTOR employees open our drawings?** No. LANXTOR support sees your account and billing data so it can help with licenses and seats, not your projects, objects, drawings or documents. Access for a support case is given only when an Owner or Administrator approves it, and everything support does is in your audit log.

**How do we get our data out?** An Owner or Administrator chooses File → Organization… → Export → Export everything…: one archive with every table as open JSON lines and every file, up to 4 GB.

**What happens when the trial ends?** The organization becomes read-only for 90 more days. Everything stays visible and can be exported; nothing is lost.

## Your data, your deployment: E1 in your own cloud or data centre

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-enterprise-deployment.html

E1 runs as a cloud service by default, and as an enterprise installation when your policy requires it. LANXTOR gives you the installation: the same E1, with your projects, drawings and documents in your own Microsoft Azure subscription or on-premises on your own servers, in your own PostgreSQL database, under your own rules. Updates install themselves in the hour you choose.

### Cloud by default, your own servers when policy requires

E1 runs in three places: in E1 Cloud, run by LANXTOR; in your own Microsoft Azure subscription; or on-premises in your own data centre. It is the same E1 in each.

Most teams start in E1 Cloud, hosted by LANXTOR in the EU. When contracts, export rules or company policy say where engineering data must be kept, an enterprise installation puts it there: data sovereignty in your own subscription, region and network. Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Alibaba Cloud are coming as further choices.

In your own Azure there are two ways to run it. Your IT installs and runs it with LANXTOR's instructions, or LANXTOR runs it in your Azure for you. Either way, the subscription, the data and the Azure bill are yours.

The status bar in E1 always names where the projects are kept, for example Microsoft Azure or PostgreSQL with the name of your database server, so everyone can see which installation they are in.

### How an installation is set up

In E1, the Owners and Administrators of your organization download everything to install E1 from their Account in E1 Cloud, under Own installation, once LANXTOR has turned it on for the organization.

The installation package is one zip: the newest release of E1, your access to E1's releases and a short Start here. Your IT unzips it in Azure Cloud Shell and follows the install steps; your own E1 is created in your subscription and prints its address. Each download asks you to confirm it is you with a passkey, and is recorded in your organization's audit log.

A new installation has no owner. Only the person whose email address was named as its operator can claim it by signing in first; nobody else can. The desktop app connects to your installation by its address, and people use it in the browser as they would E1 Cloud.

### A signed license file, checked offline

In your own installation, the plan, the seats of each license, the content packages and the dates come from a license file signed by LANXTOR. E1 checks it on its own, offline.

The Owner downloads the license file from Account → Own installation in E1 Cloud and loads it once in File → Organization… → Members, and again each time LANXTOR issues a renewed one. The plan and seats apply at once, and loading it is in the audit log. A file is bound to your installation's address. E1 refuses a file that was changed after signing, a file for another address and one that is not valid yet, and says why.

Thirty days before a license ends, every Owner and Administrator gets a notice in the Inbox. After the end comes a grace period, 30 days unless your contract says otherwise, in which everything still works. After that the installation is read-only until a renewed file is loaded: everyone can still open, view and export everything. E1 is never locked.

### Company single sign-on and directory sync

In E1, colleagues sign in with their company account through any OpenID Connect provider, and your company directory creates, updates and deactivates them in E1 with SCIM 2.0.

Owners and Administrators set up sign-on under File → Organization… → Sign-on with your IT, for example with Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Keycloak or ADFS. Sign-on works for your company's verified email domains, and Only this way makes it the one way in for them. Signing in with a company Microsoft account is also available.

Directory sync deactivates whoever leaves: their membership, license and roles end and they can no longer sign in, while their history stays. Directory groups become E1 groups, and a group can give a license, for example E1-Editors → Editor. Owners and Administrators still confirm with a passkey.

### Audit, access and integration under your rules

In E1, administrators see who did what: the Audit tab lists important events and every request sent to an AI model, and access history shows every change to members, licenses, groups and roles with before and after.

E1 support has no access to your data. When it asks for access for a support case, nothing is given until an Owner or Administrator approves it, for a few hours, read-only or with changes; it ends at once with End. Everything support does shows in history and the audit log.

Other systems connect through E1's API with access tokens and service accounts, through signed webhooks and a change feed, or through MQTT, AMQP and Kafka brokers. On your own installation a broker may be in your own network. Owners and Administrators can export the whole organization at any time, in open formats.

- Data: your own PostgreSQL database, in your subscription or data centre.
- Updates: they install themselves in the hour you choose; urgent fixes within the hour.
- Licensing: single sign-on, many licenses, one invoice.
- Exit: Export everything gives every table as JSON lines and every file.

### Questions

**Can E1 run on-premises?** Yes. Besides E1 Cloud and your own Microsoft Azure, E1 can be installed on-premises on your own servers, with your own PostgreSQL database. Contact sales to plan it.

**Which clouds can we install E1 in?** Microsoft Azure today. Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Alibaba Cloud are coming.

**Does LANXTOR hold our data in an own installation?** No. In your own Azure the subscription, the data and the bill are yours, whether your IT runs E1 or LANXTOR runs it there for you. E1 support sees your projects only if an Owner or Administrator approves a support request.

**Does E1 need to call LANXTOR to check the license?** No. The license file is signed by LANXTOR and checked by E1 itself, offline. You load a renewed file when LANXTOR issues one.

**What happens if our license file runs out?** A grace period follows, 30 days unless your contract says otherwise, in which everything works. After it the installation is read-only: everything can be opened, viewed and exported, but not changed, until the Owner loads a renewed file.

**Which sign-in providers work?** Any OpenID Connect provider, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Keycloak or ADFS, with SCIM 2.0 directory sync. Company Microsoft accounts work too.

**How are updates installed?** Updates install themselves in the hour you choose, and urgent fixes within the hour. When your server is updated, E1 in the browser and in the desktop app tells each user that a new version is ready.

## Windows and macOS desktop app, browser and tablet: one project everywhere

https://www.lanxtor.com/solution-desktop-browser-tablet.html

In E1, you engineer in the desktop app for Windows or macOS, or in the browser with nothing to install, and review from any browser on a laptop or a tablet. Every place opens the same project on the same server with the same account, so there are no files to copy and nothing to sync. A change made in one place is seen everywhere within seconds.

### The desktop app for Windows and macOS

E1 is a desktop app for Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit) and for Macs with Apple silicon on macOS 12 or newer. Both are signed and keep themselves up to date.

Download it from Get E1: your own system is offered first. The Windows app is signed by Lanxtor LLC; the Mac app is signed and notarized by Apple, so macOS shows no warning about an unidentified developer. At the first start you choose the server: Use E1 Cloud, or type the address of your organization's own server. You sign in with the same account as in the browser, and your projects are there.

In the desktop app, floating windows are real windows: take a tab out to work side by side or on a second screen, and it opens again where it was at the next start. The app looks for a new version when it starts and every four hours, downloads it in the background and asks you to restart. You never download an installer again, and an update never goes back to an older version.

### E1 in the browser, with nothing to install

In E1, the browser is a full place to work, not a reduced viewer: open app.lanxtor.com or your organization's E1 address, sign in, and the same projects open with the same tools.

The browser suits any computer, including Linux, Intel Macs and Windows on Arm, which have no desktop installer. E1 Cloud is tested with current Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. On the account page of the website, Open E1 in the browser takes you straight in.

E1 saves each change on the server as you make it. Your tabs, your selection and the rows you opened are kept for you on the server and come back after a reload; your appearance and panel widths are kept per browser. In the browser, floating windows open as pop-ups.

### Review from a laptop or a tablet

In E1, reviewers and viewers work in the real model, not in an exported PDF: a Reviewer can redline, comment and approve, and a Viewer sees everything read-only.

A Reviewer marks up a 2D space with clouds, arrows, text, pins and stamps on a Markups layer, and can never change the drawing. Each markup has a card with its discussion and status, and a review round ends with a comment resolution sheet. Viewers see every project, drawing, list and document they are given, in E1 itself. Clients and contractors invited to a project as guests view it for free.

On a tablet, E1 runs in the browser. Some screens are made for a finger: the field view of the wire moves shows each lift and land in large rows, and one tap ticks a move off with your name and the time. E1 Reviewer for iPad and E1 Mobile for iPhone are coming to the App Store, as Get E1 shows.

### The same project, the same account, wherever you are

In E1, the project lives on the server, not on a device: the desktop app and the browser are two ways into the same data.

Start a change at your desk in the desktop app and check it later from a browser in the plant or a meeting room. A change by one engineer reaches everyone who has the project open within seconds, pushed by the server, with no reload. Avatars on a 2D space's toolbar show who else has it open, and when two people change the same thing, the first change is kept and the second is refused with a clear message.

An E1 license is for one named person, and every change and approval is recorded under that name. One account may be open in up to three places at once, browsers and the desktop app together. In a fourth place, E1 asks which one to sign out.

- Desktop app: Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit); macOS 12 or newer on Apple silicon.
- Browser: current Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, on any computer or tablet.
- Servers: E1 Cloud, or your organization's own E1 installation.
- Updates: the server and the desktop app each tell you when a new version is ready.

### Questions

**Does E1 run on a Mac?** Yes. The desktop app runs on Macs with Apple silicon on macOS 12 or newer, signed and notarized by Apple. On an Intel Mac, use E1 in the browser.

**Is there a Linux version?** There is no Linux desktop app. E1 runs in the browser on Linux with nothing to install.

**Is the browser version limited compared with the desktop app?** No. Both open the same projects on the same server with the same account and tools. The desktop app adds real floating windows that reopen where they were, and its own updates.

**Can we use E1 on an iPad or another tablet?** Yes, in the browser. E1 Reviewer for iPad is coming to the App Store; until then, review on a tablet in the browser.

**Can the desktop app connect to our own server?** Yes. At the first start, choose Use E1 Cloud or type your organization's server address, for example https://e1.example.com, and click Connect. The app remembers it.

**How is the desktop app updated?** It looks for a new version at start and every four hours, downloads it in the background and asks you to restart. Check for Updates… in the app menu looks at once.

**Can I be signed in on my laptop and a tablet at once?** Yes. One account may be open in up to three places at once. In a fourth, E1 asks which place to sign out.
